summary: Introduces simple extensions to the Routing Policy Specification Language (RPSL) so it can document routing policies for IPv6 and multicast address families.

plainLanguage.summary: RPSLng extends the Routing Policy Specification Language so network registries can describe IPv6 and multicast routing policy as well as IPv4 unicast policy. New multi-protocol attributes preserve the meaning of the existing IPv4 fields.

questions: what is the afi attribute in rpsl
how to write ipv6 routing policy in rpsl
subtitle: Extensions to RPSL for documenting IPv6 and multicast routing policy.

tldr.problem: RPSL originally documented IPv4 unicast routing policy and could not distinguish policies across IPv6 and multicast address families.
tldr.mechanism: RPSLng adds mp-import, mp-export, and mp-default attributes with address-family selectors, plus IPv6 route and router data types.
tldr.outcome: The extensions preserve the original IPv4 attributes and add IPv6 and multicast policy support. RFC 4012 updates RFC 2622 and RFC 2725 and is updated by RFC 7909.

today: RFC 4012 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2005. It updates RFC 2622 and RFC 2725, and is updated by RFC 7909.

sections.title: Extending RPSL to More Address Families
sections.content:
RFC 2622 defines RPSL for IPv4 unicast routing, and RFC 2725 adds security extensions. RPSLng extends the language to document policy for IPv6 and multicast while aiming to preserve compatibility and avoid duplicate information.

The extension distinguishes four policy families: IPv4 unicast, IPv4 multicast, IPv6 unicast, and IPv6 multicast.
sections.plainLanguage: RPSLng adds ways to describe IPv6 and multicast routing policy. The existing IPv4 unicast policy fields keep their original meaning.

sections.title: Address Families and Multi-Protocol Attributes
sections.content:
The existing import, export, and default attributes continue to mean IPv4 unicast policy. The new mp-import, mp-export, and mp-default attributes can specify an address family using afi.

If no afi is supplied, the policy applies to all four families, equivalent to afi any. Where multiple specifications match a peering, the first matching specification in document order is used.
sections.plainLanguage: The mp- attributes say which address family a policy covers. If no family is named, the policy applies to IPv4 and IPv6, both unicast and multicast.

sections.title: Peerings and Route Filters
sections.content:
An mp-peering expression identifies an autonomous system and may identify routers using IPv4 or IPv6 addresses, router names, or sets. Its AND, OR, and EXCEPT operators combine or subtract groups.

An mp-filter extends the existing RPSL filter syntax to allow both IPv4 and IPv6 prefixes and prefix ranges. Address-family constraints can make a filter match no routes, for example when an IPv4 prefix is used in an IPv6-only policy.
sections.plainLanguage: A peering expression says which network or router exchanges routes. A filter says which routes are accepted or announced, and can now include IPv4 and IPv6 prefixes.

sections.title: IPv6 Route and Router Records
sections.content:
The route6 class is the IPv6 counterpart of route. Its key is the route6 prefix and origin pair, and its attributes use IPv6 prefixes or addresses where required.

Other classes gain multi-protocol fields, including mp-members, mp-filter, mp-peering, interface, and mp-peer. The inet-rtr interface field can describe IPv4 and IPv6 interfaces and tunnels using GRE or IPinIP. The dictionary also adds ipv6_address and the protocol name MPBGP.
sections.plainLanguage: A new route6 record holds an IPv6 route. Existing route-set, router, and filter records gain fields that can represent IPv6 data.

sections.title: Authorization for IPv6 Route Records
sections.content:
RPSLng extends the route authorization rules to route6 and inet6num objects. Adding a route6 object must satisfy authorization from its aut-num object and from an applicable route6 object or, if none applies, an inet6num object.

The registry searches for an exact prefix match and then a less-specific match. It uses mnt-routes when present; otherwise it may use mnt-lower or mnt-by under the rules in the RFC.
sections.plainLanguage: Adding an IPv6 route record requires authorization from both the autonomous-system record and the applicable address-space or route record. The registry checks the relevant maintainers before accepting it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says these extensions introduce no new security functionality or threats. It notes that authentication mechanisms in the original RPSL can be weak.

MAIL-FROM can be defeated by spoofing a source email address. CRYPT-PW is vulnerable to dictionary attacks and password sniffing over unencrypted channels, while NONE offers no protection for objects.
sections.plainLanguage: The extensions do not add new security threats, but the RFC warns that some existing RPSL authentication methods offer weak or no protection.
